sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: This objective is bigger. Instead of one concept, CompTIA is giving us several security foundations that show up everywhere else in Security+.
GSA breaks Objective 1.2 into separate mini-lessons under the same objective rather than throwing one giant wall of text at the student.
sections.callout: Move through one mini-lesson at a time, then use the Maestro Recognition Sheet before the Mini Check.

sections.title: CIA Triad
paragraphs: The CIA triad describes three fundamental goals of information security.

entries.title: Confidentiality
paragraphs: Think: “Who is allowed to see this?”
Controls such as encryption and access restrictions can help protect confidentiality.

entries.title: Integrity
paragraphs: Think: “Can I trust that this has not been changed?”
Integrity protects against unauthorized modification.

entries.title: Availability
paragraphs: Think: “Can I get to it when I need it?”
Availability concerns uptime and reliable access.
entries.recognitionCue: Outage or unavailable service → Availability problem

table.caption: CIA triad recognition sheet
rows: Only authorized users can see the information
Information remains accurate and unauthorized changes are prevented or detected
Authorized users can access systems and data when needed

sections.title: Non-Repudiation
paragraphs: Non-repudiation provides evidence that someone performed an action so they cannot credibly deny it later.
Think: “We can prove YOU did this.”
Digital signatures can help provide non-repudiation.
sections.callout: Cannot deny having performed an action → Non-repudiation

sections.title: AAA
paragraphs: AAA means Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting.

entries.title: Authentication
paragraphs: Who are you?
The system verifies the identity of a person or system.
A human might authenticate with credentials or MFA. A system or service may authenticate using machine credentials such as certificates or keys.
entries.recognitionCue: Authentication proves identity for people and systems

entries.title: Authorization
paragraphs: What are you allowed to do?
Authentication proves identity. Authorization determines permissions after identity has been established.

entries.title: Accounting
paragraphs: What did you do?
Accounting records activity for logging, auditing, usage tracking, and investigations.

sections.callout: Who are you? → Authentication · What can you do? → Authorization · What did you do? → Accounting

sections.title: Authorization Models
paragraphs: The objective requires students to understand authorization models, so GSA connects this foundation to models seen later in more depth, such as role-based or attribute-based access.
Authentication identifies the subject. The authorization model determines which resources and actions that subject can access.
We do not have to dump every later IAM lesson into Objective 1.2. The goal here is to establish the foundation and link forward.
sections.callout: Identity is established first; the authorization model then determines permitted access.

sections.title: Gap Analysis
paragraphs: Gap analysis compares where security is now with where security should be. The difference is the gap.
Example: The current state uses password-only authentication. The desired state uses MFA. The gap is that MFA has not yet been implemented.
sections.callout: Current state versus desired state → Gap analysis

sections.title: Zero Trust
paragraphs: Traditional security often assumes that something inside a trusted network is safer.
Zero Trust changes the mindset: do not automatically trust a user, device, or system simply because of where it is located.
Access should be continuously evaluated according to policy.
The objective divides Zero Trust into two major pieces: the control plane and the data plane.
sections.callout: Never automatically trust because of location → Zero Trust

sections.title: Zero Trust — Control Plane
paragraphs: Think of the control plane as the decision-making brain.

entries.title: Adaptive Identity
paragraphs: Identity decisions can change based on context and risk.
entries.recognitionCue: Identity decision changes with context or risk → Adaptive identity

entries.title: Threat Scope Reduction
paragraphs: Limit how far an attacker can move or how much damage a compromise can cause.
entries.recognitionCue: Reduce movement and potential damage → Threat scope reduction

entries.title: Policy-Driven Access Control
paragraphs: Access is granted according to defined policies rather than assumptions of trust.
entries.recognitionCue: Defined policy determines access → Policy-driven access control

entries.title: Policy Engine
paragraphs: The Policy Engine makes the access decision.
Think: “Should this request be allowed?”

entries.title: Policy Administrator
paragraphs: The Policy Administrator carries out or coordinates the decision made by the Policy Engine.

sections.callout: Policy Engine = decides · Policy Administrator = acts on the decision

sections.title: Zero Trust — Data Plane
paragraphs: The data plane is where the actual communication and access happen.

entries.title: Implicit Trust Zones
paragraphs: Zero Trust aims to reduce reliance on automatically trusted areas.
entries.recognitionCue: Location alone should not create automatic trust

entries.title: Subject/System
paragraphs: The subject or system is the user, device, application, or system attempting access.

entries.title: Policy Enforcement Point
paragraphs: The Policy Enforcement Point, or PEP, enforces the access decision.
entries.recognitionCue: Allows or blocks the request → Policy Enforcement Point

entries.title: Zero Trust Flow
paragraphs: Subject requests access → Policy Engine decides → Policy Administrator coordinates → Policy Enforcement Point allows or blocks.

sections.title: Physical Security
paragraphs: Every item from the official objective becomes a recognition lesson.

table.caption: Physical security recognition sheet
rows: Stop vehicles from reaching protected areas
Controlled entry area with sequential doors

sections.title: Sensors

entries.title: Infrared
paragraphs: Detects heat or infrared energy.

entries.title: Pressure
paragraphs: Detects weight or physical pressure.

entries.title: Microwave
paragraphs: Uses microwave energy to detect movement.

entries.title: Ultrasonic
paragraphs: Uses high-frequency sound waves to detect movement.

sections.callout: Exam trick: Security+ may describe how the sensor detects movement instead of naming it directly.

sections.title: Deception and Disruption Technology
paragraphs: These technologies intentionally give attackers something fake or monitored to interact with.

entries.title: Honeypot
paragraphs: A honeypot is a decoy system designed to attract attackers.

entries.title: Honeynet
paragraphs: A honeynet is a network of honeypots or decoy systems.

entries.title: Honeyfile
paragraphs: A honeyfile is a decoy file intended to attract unauthorized access.
Example: An attacker opens a tempting file named Executive_Salaries_2026.xlsx and security receives an alert.

entries.title: Honeytoken
paragraphs: A honeytoken is fake digital information designed to reveal misuse.
entries.recognitionCue: Fake data, credential, or token → Honeytoken

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
paragraphs: Use this final sheet to recognize the objective's major clues quickly.
bullets: Current state vs. desired state → Gap analysis

miniCheck.intro: Use the Zero Trust flow: identify the component that makes the decision, then identify the component that enforces it.
miniCheck.prompt: A Zero Trust access request is evaluated by one component that decides whether access should be allowed. The final decision is then applied at the access gate.
miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. The Policy Engine decides whether the request should be allowed. The Policy Enforcement Point is the gate that applies the decision by allowing or blocking access.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Follow the Zero Trust flow again: the Policy Engine decides, the Policy Administrator coordinates, and the Policy Enforcement Point enforces at the gate.
